analysis.one_liner: Tightens the federal funding cap on for-profit colleges, counting GI Bill benefits as federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 9 Democratic sponsors, referred to the Senate education committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: For-profit colleges must currently get at least 10% of their money from non-federal sources (the "90/10 rule") to qualify for federal student aid. This bill would raise that bar to 15% and count all federal money — including GI Bill benefits and veterans' education funds, which the old rule ignored — as federal money. Schools that fail would lose access to federal student aid. It also tightens what schools may count as revenue and requires an annual public report on how much of each for-profit school's income comes from taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who enroll at for-profit colleges, veterans targeted by those schools, and taxpayers who fund federal student aid. The bill aims to stop schools that live almost entirely off federal loans, grants, and GI Bill money from collecting more aid.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum share of non-federal revenue a for-profit college must have from 10% to 15%, and counts all federal funds — not just student aid under the Higher Education Act — so schools cannot pass the test using GI Bill benefits or other federal programs.

Excludes only the monthly Post-9/11 GI Bill housing stipend, so schools can no longer game the calculation with veterans' tuition and living benefits while loading students into degrees of little value.
Stops schools from counting their own institutional loans and self-funded scholarships as non-federal revenue, closing a known workaround under the old rule.
Requires the Education Department to report annually to Congress how much of each for-profit school's revenue comes from federal funds, giving students and taxpayers visibility for the first time.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies that derive most of their revenue from federal student aid and GI Bill benefits. Schools that cannot reach the 15% threshold would have to change their business or lose federal aid eligibility.

drawbacks.text: If poorly performing schools lose federal aid and close, some current students could be left mid-program, and students may have fewer convenient evening or online course options in their area.

A revenue-threshold rule measures where money comes from, not educational quality; a school could still raise tuition from private sources or cut costs to meet the 15% test without improving outcomes for students.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: less taxpayer money flowing to schools that survive on federal aid and recruit veterans for their benefits, and public disclosure of schools' federal dependence. The main cost — possible mid-program closures — is real but is the intended consequence of denying aid to schools that cannot attract non-federal revenue; the reporting requirement and the use of existing audited financial statements make the rule workable. The rule checks funding dependence rather than quality, so it is a blunt instrument, but the burden it targets is one that falls directly on students and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's education committee never took it up; it sat there until that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill with Sen. Harkin on November 6, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
Eight other Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors, for a total of nine sponsors, all Democrats.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit college companies that depend on federal student aid and GI Bill benefits kept their existing revenue stream. Students and veterans gained nothing, since the protections were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges relying on federal aid

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill, which was referred to the committee he chaired.

for.name: 8 of 100 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die at referral stage.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to tighten the 90/10 rule and count GI Bill benefits as federal revenue during this period, having lobbied against similar restrictions in prior Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where parties stood; the absence of any committee action under a Democratic chair meant no party had to take a public position.

industries.note: The bill threatens the core business of for-profit schools that collect most revenue from federal student loans, Pell Grants, and GI Bill benefits by cutting off federal aid at schools below the 15% non-federal threshold. The old rule let these schools pass while deriving 90% of revenue from taxpayers, including veterans' benefits.

industries.industry: Federal student loan and aid programs
industries.note: Taxpayers fund the aid system and currently absorb defaults from schools that depend almost entirely on federal money; the bill would deny aid to institutions that cannot attract non-federal revenue, reducing taxpayer exposure.
